items.title: South Central 90: India’s new anti-reservation drama, CM Vijay’s Parandur decision
items.summary: Was scrapping the Parandur airport project the right call for Chennai, or could the Vijay government’s decision hurt Tamil Nadu’s industrial ambitions? In this week's South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Pooja Prasanna discuss the Tamil Nadu government’s decision to scrap the Parandur airport project and the growing debate over India’s new anti-reservation movement. They are joined by aviation safety consultant Captain Mohan Ranganathan and K E Raghunathan, national chairman of the Association of Indian Entrepreneurs, to discuss Chennai’s airport plans and what the cancellation could mean for the city’s environment, connectivity and industrial growth. Captain Mohan Ranganathan says that the Parandur site posed serious flood and aviation safety concerns. He says filling around 4,000 acres with concrete could leave floodwaters with nowhere to drain. He recalls writing in 2008, when discussions first began, that "if any obstacle or obstruction is put across the river, any flooding will affect areas south, southeast and west of that”. He says that the 2015 flood was a result of this. He also flags that the soil isn't suited for a runway, and that concretising 4,000 acres would leave floodwaters nowhere to go, warning that building the airport could mean "you can forget about Chennai existing, it is going to be completely wiped out." He argues that Chennai’s existing airport could instead be made more efficient through better planning, redesign and coordination. items.title: Maharashtra family court judges cannot be treated as judicial officers for High Court elevation: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to revisit its ruling which had held that judges belonging to Maharashtra's separate family court cadre cannot be treated as holding a "judicial office" for determining eligibility for appointment as High Court judges under Article 217 of the Constitution. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a plea by seven family court judges seeking a declaration that presiding officers of family courts be treated as holding judicial office for the purposes of elevation to the High Court. CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana Senior Advocate R Basant , appearing for the petitioners, urged the Court to reconsider its 2010 ruling in ST Joshi v. High Court of Judicature at Bombay . He argued that circumstances had materially changed since, with Maharashtra having appointed only judicial officers or advocates as family court judges for the past 36 years. The Supreme Court was, however, not persuaded that this justified reopening the precedent. "So unless and until there is any change, factually or legally, why should we revisit this issue?" CJI Surya Kant asked. The Bench observed that the real difficulty arose from Maharashtra maintaining family court judges as an exclusive cadre separate from the State judicial service. "The problem lies in the creation of a separate cadre for family courts," the CJI remarked. Senior Advocate R Basant The Court contrasted Maharashtra's system with States where District Judges are posted to family courts and later return to the regular judicial service. Such officers retain their status as judicial officers and consequently, do not face the same difficulty under Article 217(2)(a). Basant contended that ST Joshi verdict itself stood in the way of Maharashtra restructuring the cadre. The Court disagreed, observing that the State Government and the Bombay High Court could reformulate the recruitment rules and encadre family court posts into the judicial service. items.title: Subhash Chandra insolvency: NCLT forms 5-member bench after lack of consensus in verdicts
items.summary: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has constituted a 5-member bench to decide the personal insolvency case against Zee Group founder Subhash Chandra after a 2-member bench held that no majority opinion had emerged on his repayment plan. The development concerns Chandra’s proposal to pay ₹6.25 crore to creditors against admitted claims of ₹22,006.57 crore. NCLT President Justice (retd) Anupinder Singh Grewal has constituted a 5-member bench comprising himself, Judicial Members Bachu Venkat Balaram Das and Mahendra Khandelwal, and Technical Members Atul Chaturvedi and Ravindra Chaturvedi. The special bench will hear the matter at 10.15 AM on September 1. On August 31, a 2-member bench comprising Judicial Member Ashok Kumar Bhardwaj and Technical Member Reena Sinha Puri held that no final order could be passed on the basis of the opinion delivered by third member Nilesh Sharma on August 25. The 2-member bench found that the 3 members had taken materially different positions on the repayment plan. Bhardwaj had originally favoured approving the plan only in relation to creditors who supported it. He proposed allowing dissenting creditors, including banks and financial institutions, to continue pursuing independent remedies for recovery of their debts. Puri, however, rejected the repayment plan after finding serious defects in the process followed by the resolution professional. Following the split verdict, the matter was referred to Judicial Member Nilesh Sharma under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013. On August 25, Sharma opined that the repayment plan should be approved. However, he excluded claims submitted through Anil Kumar on behalf of 960 individuals and Sunil Jain on behalf of 300 individuals. He directed the resolution professional to redistribute the amount allotted to these claims among the remaining eligible creditors. When the matter returned to the original 2-member bench, it held that Sharma had “consciously passed an independent order” rather than agreeing entirely with either of the two original opinions. Meanwhile, LIC Housing Finance has challenged the August 25 order before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta sought an urgent hearing on August 31, arguing that allowing the order to continue would defeat the purpose of the IBC. The appeal is also scheduled to be heard on September 1. [Read Notification]

items.title: Supreme Court panel submits nationwide roadmap to modernise court infrastructure
items.summary: A Supreme Court-appointed panel on Monday placed before Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant its interim report containing a nationwide blueprint for modernising court infrastructure across the country. The CJI had constituted the Judicial Infrastructure Advisory Committee on May 12, headed by Supreme Court Justice Aravind Kumar . Its other members include Calcutta High Court Justice Debangsu Basak , Punjab and Haryana High Court Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra , Bombay High Court Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan and Central Public Works Department Director General Satinder Pal Singh. Supreme Court Secretary General Bharat Parashar serves as the Committee’s Member Secretary. According to a press statement issued by the Supreme Court, the committee has prepared a blueprint with the purpose of securing suitable government allocation for court modernisation and to address infrastructural deficiencies through substantial financial support. The Committee examined measures for establishing modern court complexes and improving the working conditions of judicial officers and administrative staff to enhance the efficiency of the justice delivery system. Its mandate included identifying infrastructural constraints affecting the justice delivery system and suggesting facilities required for judges, court staff, lawyers, litigants and visitors. It was also tasked with recommending measures for the computerisation of courts under the e-Courts initiative, proposing citizen-centric services to make justice delivery more inclusive and suggesting steps to bridge the digital divide.

items.title: Rajasthan High Court Acting Chief Justice SP Sharma opts himself out of judicial work
items.summary: The Rajasthan High Court acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma has decided to opt himself out from hearing cases following protests against him by lawyers According to the new roster finalised by Justice Sharma, no bench has been constituted which includes him and no regular judicial sittings have been assigned to him from September 1 to September 5. The new roster also provides for cases earlier assigned to the acting Chief Justice to be dealt with by other benches. The change comes amid protests by lawyers demanding that Justice Sharma be divested of his charge and that a permanent Chief Justice be appointed to the High Court. Earlier today, the Rajasthan High Court Lawyers Association announced a complete strike till September 6 after an emergency general house meeting on Monday. The association also decided to send representations to Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and the President of India. The strike had followed protests by advocates at both the Jaipur and Jodhpur benches of the High Court against Justice Sharma, during which police were called in to disperse lawyers at the Jaipur premises. Visuals from the protests showed advocates raising slogans against Justice Sharma, including one alleging that “our chief is a thief.” EXCLUSIVE: Supreme Court Justice Sandeep Mehta asks CJI Surya Kant to replace Rajasthan HC Acting Chief Justice for misusing office The protests followed allegations made by Supreme Court Justice Sandeep Mehta against Justice Sharma. As first reported by Bar & Bench, Justice Mehta had written to the CJI alleging manipulation of case listings and misuse of administrative powers by Justice Sharma. He had also sought the appointment of a Chief Justice from another State to head the Rajasthan High Court with immediate effect. The CJI subsequently said that the Collegium was examining the allegations and that Justice Sharma would be given an opportunity to respond before any conclusion was reached. The letter triggered protests by lawyers who have now demanded that Justice Sharma be kept away from his duties as acting Chief Justice.

items.title: Madras HC co-opts former judge, lawyer as women members of State Bar Council
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Monday nominated retired Justice VM Velumani and advocate Sudarshana Sundar as two women members to be co-opted into the Bar Council of Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. The nominations were made by Chief Justice of the Madras High Court, Justice SA Dharmadhikari after consultation with the elected members of the State Bar Council, a communication issued by the High Court Registrar General Deepthi Arivunithi said. Justice Velumani had served as a judge of the Madras High Court before being transferred to the Calcutta High Court, from where she retired in April 2024. The move follows the Supreme Court’s August 4 order in Yogamaya MG v Union of India , along with connected proceedings, concerning the representation of women advocates in State Bar Councils. The Court had empowered Chief Justices of the respective High Courts to nominate two women members to the State Bar Councils. The apex court’s directions came against the backdrop of concerns over inadequate representation of women in the elected bodies governing the legal profession. The Court’s mechanism envisaged co-option of women members , with the process involving consultation with elected members of the respective State Bar Councils. The High Court had earlier, through a letter dated August 21, placed the matter before the Chief Justice after the Supreme Court directions. The Chief Justice subsequently directed that a meeting be convened on August 24, following which the nominations were finalised. The Registrar General has now requested the Secretary of the Bar Council to take necessary further steps to give effect to the nominations.

items.title: Delhi HC refuses to interfere as woman chooses to stay in Adhyatmik Vidyalaya ashram against parents’ wishes
items.summary: The Delhi High Court today declined to interfere with a woman's decision to reside in an ashram against her parents' wishes [ Dumpala Meenavathi and Anr. Vs Union of India and Ors .]. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia said that it cannot direct the woman to visit her parents in violation of her right to freedom of movement and residence at one's place of choice under Article 19 of the Constitution. items.title: Delhi HC reduces punishment against DU law student accused of cheating on exam in urinal
items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently set aside a Delhi University (DU) order cancelling all papers of an LL.B. student accused of using unfair means during an exam. Justice Jasmeet Singh held that the punishment cancelling all papers for the semester was not proportionate. "In my opinion, the cancellation of the papers of the entire semester is not proportional, as even on preponderance of probability, it has not been proved that the petitioner was found using the material for copying or cheating in the paper," the Court order stated. Justice Jasmeet Singh The petitioner was appearing for the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita paper on January 13, 2025, when he stepped out to use the washroom. A faculty member followed him and allegedly found him cheating from a slip at the urinal. A show cause notice followed and the University's Examination Disciplinary Committee began an unfair means inquiry. The Committee initially debarred him from all exams till the end of the following semester under Clause C of the applicable guidelines. On appeal, the Committee reduced this to Clause B, resulting in cancellation of all papers for that semester. The petitioner challenged this before the High Court. The University had already declared his results in every subject except the paper in which the unfair means case was registered. The Court found that the inquiry report contained no statement from the faculty member stating that the petitioner was found using the material. It reiterated that such inquiries are tested on preponderance of probability, not proof beyond reasonable doubt. However, even on that standard, it noted that actual use of the material was not shown. Since the report only showed that material was found in the washroom, the petitioner was entitled to the benefit of doubt, the Court said. Therefore, it held that the case instead fell under Clause A, a lesser punishment involving cancellation of only the specific paper, with the student deemed to have scored zero in that paper. The petitioner was represented by advocates Deepak Janghu, Ankush Yadav, Karan Thobhani and Sarthak Mahajan. Delhi University was represented by advocates Amanpreet Singh and Harpreet Singh. items.title: Supreme Court dismisses plea against appointment of Justice PK Mishra’s son as Rajasthan AAG
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday dismissed a plea challenging the appointment of Padmesh Mishra, son of sitting Supreme Court Justice Prashant Kumar Mishra , as an Additional Advocate General (AAG) for Rajasthan. A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi dismissed the petition, which had challenged a Rajasthan High Court order upholding Mishra's appointment. Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi According to the plea, Mishra was enrolled as an advocate in August 2019. He was appointed as a panel lawyer at the Supreme Court on August 20, 2024, a post that required a minimum of five years’ practice. Three days later, on August 23, 2024, the Rajasthan government amended its litigation policy of 2018 to insert a new clause allowing “the authority of the appropriate level” to appoint “any counsel to any post,” after considering the counsel’s expertise, regardless of the policy’s other eligibility conditions. On that very same day, the government withdrew Mishra’s appointment as panel lawyer, and instead appointed him as AAG before the Supreme Court, a post that otherwise required ten years of practice under the same policy. The petition also argued that the appointment had been made without effective consultation with the Advocate General as required under the litigation policy, and without any objective criteria to assess Mishra’s claimed “expertise” under the newly inserted clause. items.title: AI-generated work can get copyright but AI system cannot be author: Indian copyright office
items.summary: An artificial intelligence (AI) system cannot be recognised as an author under the Copyright Act, 1957, the Copyright Office has ruled while rejecting an application that named the AI system DABUS as the author of an artwork. However, Registrar of Copyrights Dr. Unnat P Pandit clarified that a work generated through AI or computational processes could satisfy the originality requirement under copyright law. The ruling came on an application filed by American computer scientist Stephen L Thaler for registration of copyright in an artwork titled A Recent Entrance to Paradise . The application identified the Device for the Autonomous Bootstrapping of Unified Sentience (DABUS) as the author and Thaler as the copyright owner. The Copyright Office concluded that Thaler, rather than DABUS, was the person who caused the artwork to be created within the meaning of Section 2(d)(vi) of the Act. “DABUS is not a natural or juristic person recognised in law and cannot be entered as author under Section 2(d)(vi) ,” the Registrar held. Section 2(d)(vi) provides that the author of a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work is “the person who causes the work to be created”. According to Thaler, DABUS autonomously generated the artwork after being trained using photographs taken by him, curated thesaurus entries and English sentences. He argued that while he designed and configured the system, DABUS performed the core generative process and produced the final visual expression without real-time human intervention or a text prompt. The Copyright Office rejected the argument that the entity performing the final computational step must consequently be treated as the author. It noted that DABUS had not designed its architecture, selected its training methodology or supplied its inputs independently. All these processes were undertaken by Thaler. “ Autonomy in execution is not synonymous with conception of a work ,” the Registrar observed. The order added that copyright law recognises the “mastermind” behind a work rather than the autonomy of the tool used to produce it. Registrar held, “ The law recognizes the mastermind behind the creation of the work, not the autonomy of the tool through which that creation is implemented .” The Copyright Office also rejected the analogy drawn between DABUS and companies or Hindu idols, which may be treated as juristic persons in law. items.title: Bar association not state under Article 12, bar issues not subject to writ jurisdiction: J&K High Court
items.summary: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh on Monday observed that it cannot invoke its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India to settle the internal election disputes of a Bar Association [ Advocate Abdul Basit Bhat V/s District Bar Association, Shopian ]. Pertinently, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal held that a bar association or bar body is not “State” within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution and writ jurisdiction can't be invoked against it. The Court made the observation while dismissing a writ petition challenging the Shopian District Bar Association's decision to modify the eligibility criteria for lawyers to contest elections to the posts of its officer bearers. " The District Bar Association, Shopian is not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of this Court in respect of the dispute raised in the present petition. The controversy pertains to the internal affairs and electoral governance of a voluntary association and does not involve the discharge of any public duty or disclose the existence of a public-law element. The challenge to the eligibility conditions prescribed for holding office under the Constitution of the Association, therefore, does not warrant interference in the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. Accordingly, the writ petition is dismissed as not maintainable," the Court ruled. Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal The Court observed that a District Bar Association, being a voluntary association of advocates governed by its own Constitution and bye-laws, is neither a statutory body nor “State” within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. Disputes concerning such a body's internal affairs are, therefore, not amenable to the High Court's writ jurisdiction, the Court held. Writ jurisdiction is a public law remedy that can be invoked when the State acts in a manner that violates a person's rights. "The jurisdiction under Article 226 is essentially a public law remedy. It is not intended to adjudicate every dispute arising between members of a private association and the association itself," the Court explained. Muslim women in Kerala are pushing back against the Grand Mufti of India, Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar, after his remarks advocating restrictions on women’s participation in public life sparked widespread criticism on social media. Through videos and posts, women have challenged his views stating that such restrictions have no place in Kerala’s public life. The controversy began after the Kanthapuram-led faction of Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama recently issued a circular directing madrasas and local committees to bar women from public stages and prevent them from mixing with unrelated men at religious events. Defending the circular at a conference in Kochi, Kanthapuram said bringing women onto public platforms would lead to “great destruction” and argued that women should remain confined to their homes. His remarks triggered a wave of criticism, particularly from Muslim women and content creators on social media. Content creator Raseena Noushad criticised the idea that women’s role should be restricted to the home. “They believe women should stay at home, deliver babies, and cook,” she said. Turning the argument around, she asked men who oppose women entering public spaces to consider staying at home themselves. “To those who think women shouldn't go out, why don't you go to the Taliban? Why are you trying to make Kerala like the Taliban?” she asked. items.title: Activist Ravichandran (Raees) says sanitation work contracts should be shifted to Dalit entrepreneurs
items.summary: For years, sanitation workers have been at the bottom of the chain when it comes to the sanitation business. They clean public toilets, empty septic tanks and maintain public facilities, while the contracts often remain in the hands of others. Ravichandran Bathran ( Raees Mohammed) wants to change that. A Dalit man engaged in sanitation work and the founder of Dalit Camera, an organisation that has documented the lives and struggles of Dalit communities, Raees argues that government contracts related to sanitation could offer workers an opportunity to move from wage labour to entrepreneurship. But he says that cannot happen unless the tendering process itself becomes more transparent. Tamil Nadu has taken steps towards greater transparency in public procurement, including the expansion of e-tendering. The newly formed Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government has also spoken about improving transparency and accountability in government contracts. Raees, however, argues that these reforms should extend to smaller contracts, many of which are still handled through offline tender-cum-auction processes. In an interview with TNM, he explains why he believes public toilets, parking spaces, municipal shops and other revenue-generating properties should be brought under a transparent online system and why sanitation workers should get a fair chance to compete for them. Who currently controls sanitation-related contracts such as for public toilets? It is important to clarify that this is not simply a caste issue. For example, in Kotagiri and Ooty municipalities, Arunthathiyars (SC) are running public toilets. However, in Kotagiri municipality, one family has controlled the contract for 20 years. The situation is different in larger towns. In Coimbatore, Puliyampatti and several other cities, non-SC persons hold the contracts, while SC persons are employed only as cleaners. In the Nilgiris, caste discrimination is less rigid compared to other parts of Tamil Nadu, and it is not a highly crowded urban district. Many dominant castes do not see public toilet management as a lucrative business and continue to view it as a stigmatised occupation. They often have other sources of income such as estates, government jobs, factories, vehicles or real estate. items.summary: Two Malayali women were found dead at two separate apartment complexes in the Milpitas and San Jose areas of California within minutes of each other on Friday, August 28. The two locations are about a 17-minute drive apart. While the Milpitas Police arrested a 32-year-old woman after a fatal hit-and-run involving one of the women, relatives of the victims have alleged that the same woman was responsible for the second death, which San Jose Police are investigating as a homicide. The victims have been identified by their relatives as Anjana Hari, 35, from Mannuthy in Thrissur, and Ann Mary Mathew, 40, from Kesavadasapuram in Thiruvananthapuram. Neither Milpitas Police nor the San Jose Police Department (SJPD) have publicly released the identities of the victims or suspects. The two incidents were reported minutes apart. Milpitas Police said officers responded at 12.01 pm to a hit-and-run in the parking lot of Mill Creek Apartments at 440 Dixon Landing Road. Less than two hours later, at approximately 1.53 pm, San Jose Police responded to a suspicious-circumstances call in the 700 block of Linda Vista Street, where they found an unconscious woman inside a residence. Police found the victim with significant injuries and she was pronounced dead at the scene. items.title: The high cost of being trans in India, and how a new law could add to it
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Megha*, a transgender woman from northern Kerala, got her transgender ID card in 2020, five years before undergoing gender affirmation surgery. Esha Kishore, another trans activist based in Kerala, got hers in 2015, also before undergoing gender-affirming procedures. The card is the legal document that certifies an individual’s gender identity under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and neither had to undergo surgery to get it. They could apply based on their self-identification, with any medical procedures they choose to undergo coming later. Megha spent roughly Rs 3-4 lakh on her gender-affirming care, including surgery, hormone therapy, doctors' fees, tests, travel, accommodation, food, and medication. She still spends over Rs 2,000 a month on medicines, a cost she will have to shell out for decades to come, since doctors advise most trans individuals to stay on hormone therapy until their 50s. Esha too spent a comparable amount on gender affirmation procedures, which she began a decade earlier than Megha. For many like them, legal recognition did not depend on whether, when, or how they chose to medically transition. But that has now changed. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026, which came into force in May, removes statutory recognition of self-identification and requires a medical board to certify a person’s transgender identity. It also narrows the definition of who can be legally recognised as transgender, covering certain socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani, and jogta, as well as people with specified intersex variations. A heavily criticised provision also includes a separate category of people whom the law says have been compelled to adopt or present a transgender identity “by force, allurement, inducement, deceit or undue influence.” The amendment effectively excludes people whose identities are based solely on self-perception, including self-perceived trans-masculine, trans-feminine, and gender-non-binary identities. The change has left transgender persons, activists, and lawyers concerned about who will now be able to obtain legal recognition, and what the new medical-board process will require. items.title: Jaipur Dialogues —a platform that doxxed 15-year-old protestor—has BJP ties
items.summary: In late July 2026, an online storm upended the life of a 15-year-old girl. The teenager had joined the student demonstrations that forced the former Education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Like many young protesters around her, she directed her ire at Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A video clip of her comments went viral. Then came the targeted harassment campaign. Leading the charge was an organisation called The Jaipur Dialogues. Founded by Sanjay Dixit, a former Indian Administrative Services officer, it describes itself as a “vibrant online platform that aims to promote Indic knowledge systems.” In a series of posts on X, The Jaipur Dialogues’ handle sought the girl’s identifying details, branded her “most wanted”, and eventually, doxxed her. The 15-year-old protester faced threats of rape, murder, and acid attacks. Strangers showed up at her home. Her family and she went into hiding. The Jaipur Dialogues defended its actions as those of a “responsible nationalist platform” in an article it published on August 1. “We posted those images on our X handle, demanded public identification of those who crossed every line of decency, and were fully prepared to back legal action,” the article said . “If demanding accountability for open contempt of the Prime Minister of India makes Jaipur Dialogues guilty in the eyes of the left, we wear that guilt proudly.” The organisation’s conduct towards the teenager brought its wider content under scrutiny. The Jaipur Dialogues’ website—which has sections such as “Islam” and “Sanatana”—publishes stories that are often propagandist and communal. Consider some recent examples: a piece that is headlined “Demographic Jihad claims another locality in Gujarat”, and another that frames Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay’s decision to challenge the state ban on cow slaughter as a “blatant nod to minority vote-bank appeasement”. Its social media handles routinely target public figures who are Christian or Muslim. items.title: When discounts cost dearly: Why Bengaluru restaurants are upset with Swiggy, Zomato
items.summary: Shangrila, a Tibetan restaurant on Bengaluru’s Brigade Road, is 52 years old. Currently managed by Kunga, a third generation owner, the restaurant never needed advertising to attract customers. Rather, word of mouth did that job for no charge. Then online platform for food delivery Swiggy came along eight years ago and started taking 24-25% of every order. Around six months ago, the restaurant stopped its association with the delivery platform. Kunga says money wasn’t really the reason. It was how Swiggy treated the relationship. Nobody from the company ever came by to ask how the restaurant was doing. Kunga’s is not the only food business in Bengaluru with a soured relationship with delivery platforms. Restaurant owners across the city accuse both Swiggy and Zomato of charging high commissions and applying discounts and other hidden charges without prior intimation, let alone contractual agreements. They say that commissions and hidden charges cost them Rs 40-60 for every Rs 100 worth of orders. Discontent over the charges levied by delivery platforms have been simmering among businesses for several months now. With the added pressures of the LPG crisis , it boiled over, prompting the Bangalore Hotels Association to call for a boycott of these platforms. The threat of a boycott brought Swiggy and Zomato to the table for discussions with the association, held on August 6 and 7. For now, both delivery platforms have agreed to seek restaurant consent before activating promotions and relook into past campaigns that were run without approval. Although restaurant owners had initially announced a complete boycott from August 15, they later set an August 31 deadline for assessing whether their concerns have been resolved. TNM met with restaurateurs from different parts of the city to understand how the allegedly predatory pricing and steep deductions by delivery platforms eat into their profits. While owners of legacy restaurants say an established customer base keeps them immune to the threats of delivery platforms to a large extent, newer entrants are forced to pay large sums to the platforms in commission and advertisement, while struggling to find a footing in the industry. ‘It’s never 30%’ Restaurants typically pay platforms a commission on orders generated through them.
